speaker: Max Levchin
title: Max Levchin - Building Affirm, PayPal, and Why He Only Starts Network Businesses
question: In consumer fintech, what structural inflection points push a scaled company using bank partners to pursue its own bank charter?
guest: We said for a long time that we don't need a bank charter to do what we do, and we have many excellent bank partnerships. We operate as a bank partner issuer, collaborating with several banks where we're subject to their policies and their regulatory oversight, and we have to explain ourselves to their regulators through them. There are two reasons to apply for a bank charter. First, you get sophisticated enough where you want your own regulatory relationships and want to speak to your regulators directly. As we get larger and keep growing—taking share from point-of-sale wallet share and other financial instruments like credit and debit cards—at some point having a direct relationship with your regulators goes from a nice-to-have to a requirement. Second, there will be a day when you want to offer a feature, a collection of features, or a new product that legally requires you to be a bank. We've successfully avoided that need by not delving into products only banks can offer, but that isn't necessarily true forever, so a charter lets us expand into features that require one.

points.core: Partner-bank fintechs must communicate with financial regulators indirectly through their sponsoring banks.
points.note: Accept: explaining that bank-partner issuers are subject to partner policies and explain themselves to regulators via those partner banks. Do not credit: generic claims that fintechs are heavily regulated.

points.core: Reaching major market scale turns direct regulatory relationships into an operational requirement.
points.note: Accept: noting that as a fintech grows large and takes significant wallet share, speaking directly to regulators shifts from nice-to-have to necessary. Do not credit: vague statements that charters improve credibility.

points.core: Holding a charter unlocks regulated financial products legally restricted to licensed banks.
points.note: Accept: explaining that a charter enables future features or product lines (e.g., bank-only offerings) unavailable under non-bank structures. Do not credit: generic mentions of expanding product offerings without the legal/charter requirement.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A scaled fintech typically seeks its own charter when the partner-bank model shifts from an enabler to a constraint, and several pressures tend to converge.

The first is balance-sheet economics. Once lending volume is large, funding loans through warehouse lines, forward-flow sales, or partner balance sheets costs far more than insured deposits, and the company gives up net interest margin to the partner. SoFi and LendingClub both cited cheaper deposit funding and holding loans on balance sheet as core rationales.

The second is revenue-share leakage: at scale, the fees and interest split paid to sponsor banks exceed the fixed cost of running a regulated bank.

The third is concentration and regulatory risk. Consent orders against sponsor banks and the Synapse collapse showed that a partner's compliance problems can freeze growth or product launches, and regulators increasingly treat the fintech as accountable anyway, so it bears the compliance burden without the control.

The fourth is product and strategic control: direct payment-rail access, faster launches, a uniform national lending framework without "true lender" exposure, and customer primacy.

A receptive chartering climate usually sets the timing.

points.why: The response describes exposure to sponsor-bank compliance problems without explaining that the fintech communicates with regulators through its sponsor banks.
The response links scale to funding and revenue-sharing economics without explaining why growth makes direct regulatory relationships operationally necessary.
The response cites insured deposits as cheaper funding without identifying a feature or product the fintech could legally offer only with a bank charter.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Scaled consumer fintechs pursue a bank charter when the cost, risk, and friction of renting a sponsor bank’s balance sheet outweigh the capital and regulatory burdens of direct supervision. The primary inflection point is funding economics: as monetization shifts from interchange toward lending, replacing costly, volatile warehouse lines and securitization markets with low-cost insured deposits expands net interest margins and stabilizes credit supply during downturns. At scale, these lending gains and eliminated partner-bank fees outweigh losing Durbin Amendment debit interchange exemptions above $10 billion in assets.

Operational and regulatory control drive the transition further. A charter grants direct access to Federal Reserve payment rails, federal preemption of state licensing and interest-rate caps, and faster product launches without third-party compliance bottlenecks. Finally, intense regulatory scrutiny on Banking-as-a-Service sponsors turns partner concentration into an existential risk; when a sponsor bank’s consent order or asset cap can abruptly freeze onboarding or throttle volume, owning a charter shifts from margin optimization to essential business continuity.

points.why: The response describes sponsor-bank compliance bottlenecks without explaining that the fintech communicates with regulators through its sponsors.
The response links scale to lending economics and sponsor risk without explaining how growth makes direct regulatory relationships necessary.
The response identifies taking insured deposits onto the fintech’s own balance sheet as a legally restricted banking activity that a charter enables.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A scaled fintech usually seeks its own charter when the bank-partner setup starts costing more than it saves.

**Funding economics.** Once a lender is big enough, funding loans with warehouse lines or securitizations costs much more than funding them with its own insured deposits. SoFi and LendingClub got charters mainly to capture net interest margin instead of renting it.

**Economics that outgrow the partner model.** Revenue-sharing with the partner bank and the Durbin interchange exemption (it only covers banks under $10 billion in assets) work at small scale. Large deposit bases can outgrow small partner banks, and splitting the revenue costs more each year as volume grows.

**Partner concentration and regulatory risk.** From 2023 to 2024, regulators issued many consent orders against partner banks, and the Synapse collapse showed how fragile the "rent-a-charter" model is. Partners can freeze onboarding or new products, or exit, with little notice.

**Legal and product limits.** "True lender" challenges to rate exportation, state-by-state licensing, and partners' limited appetite for risk all restrict products. A charter brings federal preemption and direct payment-rail access.

**Timing and maturity.** Supervision was more receptive in 2025–26, with OCC conditional approvals and a wave of fintech applications. Companies also need enough profitability, capital, and compliance infrastructure to handle bank-level oversight. Owning the balance sheet usually supports a better valuation story too.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Scaled consumer fintechs typically pursue a bank charter when the marginal costs and constraints of partner-bank arrangements outweigh the heavy capital and compliance burden of direct regulation. The primary inflection point is lending scale: once credit becomes a core revenue driver, funding loans through warehouse lines, securitizations, or partner balance sheets proves expensive and volatile, whereas a charter unlocks low-cost retail deposits and full net interest margin capture. Simultaneously, partner fee drag—spanning interchange splits, BIN-sponsorship fees, and revenue shares—grows linearly with volume until it exceeds the fixed overhead of operating a bank. Operational and regulatory bottlenecks also accelerate the shift. Sponsor banks face concentration limits, asset-size thresholds like the Durbin Amendment's $10 billion cap, and heightened supervisory scrutiny over third-party oversight that can abruptly throttle onboarding or product launches. Finally, direct ownership eliminates partner veto power over underwriting and roadmaps while granting uniform national rate exportation and direct access to payment rails, turning banking infrastructure from a rented constraint into a defensible economic moat.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A scaled fintech starts to consider a bank charter when the economics of owning the balance sheet and the value of controlling the customer experience outweigh the costs of running a regulated bank.

The clearest financial trigger is a large, recurring lending business alongside a customer base that can supply stable deposits. Funding loans with those deposits can lower funding costs, reduce reliance on warehouse lines and loan sales, and let the fintech retain more of the lending margin. At sufficient volume, fees and revenue shared with sponsor banks also become material.

The operational trigger comes when sponsor-bank approvals, risk limits, or systems regularly constrain product launches, underwriting, or service. Dependence on a partner becomes more consequential as more customers rely on the fintech for everyday banking and a partner exit could disrupt that relationship.

A charter becomes viable when those benefits can cover the ongoing cost of holding capital and liquidity, maintaining bank-grade compliance and risk controls, and operating under direct supervision. Customer scale matters because it can make that trade-off work.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A charter becomes attractive when the economics of owning a bank and the value of controlling its products outweigh the fixed costs of running one. There’s no universal customer threshold. The strongest signal is a durable base of customer deposits alongside enough recurring loan demand to put those deposits to work. Funding loans with insured deposits can cost less than relying on wholesale credit, and holding loans can let the fintech retain more interest income while taking on the associated credit risk.

A second inflection point comes when the partner bank’s approval process, risk limits, or willingness to renew the relationship starts to constrain core products. A charter gives the fintech more control over pricing, underwriting, and launches. Pursuing one makes sense when those constraints materially affect growth or continuity and the company has the earnings, capital, liquidity, and risk management to withstand losses and meet direct regulatory obligations.
